section.title: The Sayings of King Lemuel
section.sectionRationale: A second distinct voice closes the book alongside Agur, King Lemuel, otherwise unknown, whose oracle is explicitly credited to the instruction his mother taught him. It warns a young ruler against squandering strength on women and wine, and calls him instead to open his mouth for the voiceless, the poor, and the needy.
section.thesis: A king's strength is not for indulgence in women or wine but for defending the rights of the oppressed, the poor, and the needy, a charge a mother pressed on her royal son and one every person entrusted with any authority is called to imitate.
section.frameNote: Two clusters: a mother's warning against squandered strength; a mother's charge to speak for the voiceless and judge righteously.

verses.text: These are the words of King Lemuel, the burden that his mother taught him:

What shall I say, O my son? What, O son of my womb? 
What, O son of my vows?
Do not spend your strength on women or your vigor on those who ruin kings.

It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, 
or for rulers to crave strong drink,
lest they drink and forget what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice.
Give strong drink to one who is perishing, and wine to the bitter in soul.
Let him drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.

units.label: A mother's charge
units.note: speak for the voiceless, judge righteously

verses.text: Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the {{dal|dispossessed}}.
Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy.

dal.gloss: Poor, weak, dispossessed, the socially and economically vulnerable. Verse 8 charges the king to open his mouth for this class of people who have no voice of their own, an obligation that runs throughout the Torah and the Prophets and finds its ultimate model in the true King who came to bring good news to the poor.

basic.context: This short oracle preserves a mother's instruction to her royal son, King Lemuel, otherwise unknown in Scripture. She warns him plainly against squandering his strength on women who ruin kings and against the drunkenness that would make him forget justice, and then charges him with his true calling: to open his mouth for the voiceless, the poor, and the needy.
basic.hermeneutics: This is direct, personal instruction from a mother to a son who happens to be a king, applying with particular force to anyone in a position of authority, though its call to defend the voiceless and needy binds every reader regardless of rank. The permission to give strong drink to the perishing, verses 6 to 7, is not a general endorsement of drunkenness but a specific, almost medicinal exception contrasted sharply with the king's own required sobriety.
basic.originalLanguages: The dal, poor or dispossessed, verse 8, names those without social power to advocate for themselves, the very reason a king's mouth, his authority and voice, must be opened on their behalf. The mother's threefold repetition, 'my son... son of my womb... son of my vows,' verse 2, intensifies the urgency and intimacy of her charge, a vow apparently made to God concerning this son before his birth.
basic.typology: Lemuel's charge to open his mouth for the voiceless and defend the poor and needy, verses 8-9, anticipates the ministry of Christ, who was anointed to preach good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and who is the true King whose reign is finally marked by perfect justice for the oppressed. The warning against a king's self-indulgence, verses 3-5, anticipates the greater King who, though entitled to everything, emptied Himself rather than indulge Himself, Philippians 2:6-7.
basic.christ: Lemuel's charge to open his mouth for the voiceless and defend the poor and needy, verses 8-9, is fulfilled in Jesus, the true King who announced His mission as bringing good news to the poor and setting the oppressed free, Luke 4:18, and who consistently used His voice and authority on behalf of those with none of their own. And where Lemuel is warned against squandering royal strength on self-indulgence, verses 3-5, Christ, though truly a king entitled to glory, emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7, the perfect reversal of every self-serving ruler this oracle warns against.
basic.god: God's own concern for the voiceless, the poor, and the needy stands behind this charge to the king, since Scripture consistently reveals a God who hears the cry of the oppressed and holds rulers accountable for how they treat the powerless. He also cares about the ordinary integrity of a ruler's private life, strength, sobriety, and self-control, not merely public policy, since character and justice cannot finally be separated.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:18 fulfills the charge to bring good news to the poor. Philippians 2:6-7 fulfills the pattern of a king who empties himself rather than indulging himself. Psalm 72:1-4 echoes a king's calling to defend the afflicted and needy. Isaiah 1:17 echoes the charge to defend the cause of the oppressed.
basic.oneStory: A mother's charge to her son the king, to guard his strength, his sobriety, and above all his voice on behalf of the voiceless, sketches the pattern of righteous rule the whole Bible is waiting for. That pattern is fulfilled in Jesus, the true King who did not squander His glory in self-indulgence but poured Himself out to bring justice and good news to the poor.

context.literary:
Proverbs 31:1-9 is a self-contained oracle, set apart from what comes before and after by its own title in verse 1. It sits second in the closing appendix of the book, after the words of Agur in Proverbs 30, and it carries the same label, the 'burden', the very word Agur's section also used in Proverbs 30:1. The final chapter of Proverbs therefore holds two foreign-sounding voices, a thinker who confesses his limits and a mother who gives orders, and then closes with the poem about the capable woman.

The oracle is built as a single speech from a mother to a son. Its opening in verse 2 is a stammer of tenderness: three questions, each naming the son in a different way, with the mother seeming to search for the right words and finding only love and urgency. The speech then moves in two panels. Verses 3 to 7 are warnings about what a king must not pour himself into, and verses 8 and 9 are the charge about what he must give himself to. The hinge is the little word 'lest' in verse 5, which names the real danger: not the wine itself but the forgetting of 'what is decreed' and the cost to the oppressed.

The two panels are bound together by a mirror. In verse 5 the drunk king 'deprives' the oppressed of justice. In verses 8 and 9 the sober king opens his mouth for them. The verse 6 and 7 aside about strong drink for the perishing is a deliberate foil: a dying or heartbroken man may drink to dull his pain, but a ruler may not, because a ruler's judgment is other people's lifeline.

Note the repetition of 'open your mouth' at the start of both verse 8 and verse 9. It is a parallelism that becomes a drumbeat. The king's mouth, which is tempted to the cup, is called to the courtroom. And the speech ends with the three kinds of people the king is to protect, the voiceless, the dispossessed and the poor and needy, so that the opening picture of a mother and the closing picture of the powerless frame one theme: strength given to a person is strength owed to others.
context.historical:
The oracle names King Lemuel and then says nothing more about him. No king of Israel or Judah has that name, which is why readers have long guessed. Some think it is a pet name for Solomon, but the text never says so and that is a guess. Others note that Proverbs 30:1 and 31:1 both use the word translated 'burden', and that Massa was a son of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13-14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30. On that reading Lemuel may be a king of an Arabian tribe of Massa, and the translation 'burden' would be a place name. The Hebrew allows either, and the BSB follows the first reading. In either case Proverbs preserves wise counsel that reached Israel from outside its own court, which fits the way the book elsewhere gathers sayings from several hands, Proverbs 25:1.

What the passage does tell us is who taught the king. In the ancient world a court was ruled partly by the queen mother, and Israel's own books show how much weight she carried. Bathsheba sits at the king's right hand in 1 Kings 2:19, and Maacah is removed from her place as queen mother in 1 Kings 15:13 when she goes bad. Proverbs 1:8 had already told every son not to forsake 'the teaching of your mother', using the same word, torah, that is used for the father's instruction. Lemuel's mother is therefore not a soft voice at the edge of the household. She is the first and most direct instructor of a young man who will hold power.

The warnings fit a royal world. Eastern courts were famous for harems, feasts and flattery, and rulers who lived for pleasure left the poor to the mercy of corrupt officials. Deuteronomy 17:17 had already told Israel's king that he must not take many wives, 'lest his heart go astray', and Solomon's later fall in 1 Kings 11:1-4 shows how real the warning was. The poor had no lawyers; their only protection was a king, or a judge on the king's behalf, who would hear them at the gate. If that man was drunk, nobody else could speak for the powerless.
context.canonical:
The oracle reaches back to the Torah's picture of a godly king and forward to the prophets' demand for justice. Deuteronomy 17:14-20 set the pattern: a king who must not multiply wives or wealth and who must read God's instruction all his days. Lemuel's mother, without mentioning the law, preaches the same message to her son. Proverbs itself repeats the theme in nearly every section that speaks of rulers. 'By justice a king brings stability to the land,' Proverbs 29:4, and 'A king who judges the poor with fairness, his throne will be established forever,' Proverbs 29:14. Verse 8 matches Proverbs 24:11-12, which asks whether anyone who sees people stumbling toward the slaughter can plead ignorance before the God who weighs hearts.

The warning against drink has close company. Proverbs 20:1 calls wine a mocker and strong drink a brawler, and Isaiah 5:22-23 pronounces woe on those who are heroes at drinking wine while they acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice. Isaiah is describing the exact scene Lemuel's mother fears: the drinking class and the perverted courtroom are the same people.

The call to be a mouth for the voiceless is the thread running through the great royal psalm, Psalm 72. There the king is to judge God's afflicted with justice and 'deliver the needy who cry out', Psalm 72:2, 12. Job protested his innocence by saying he was 'eyes to the blind' and 'a father to the needy', Job 29:15-16. The prophets later say that God Himself defends those the king neglects.

In the New Testament the pattern lands on Jesus. He opens His public ministry by reading that He has been anointed 'to preach good news to the poor', Luke 4:18, and the Gospels show Him giving His mouth to the voiceless, the leper, the widow, the child. In Matthew 25:35-40 the King Himself says that what was done for 'the least of these' was done for Him. James picks up the same note when he calls pure religion caring for orphans and widows, James 1:27.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The compiler of Proverbs closes the book with a mother's voice because he wants the reader to see where good rule begins: in a household, at a table, in the teaching a child receives long before any crown is placed on his head. The first hearers were meant to learn three things from the oracle.

First, authority is a trust, not a prize. The strength and vigor of verse 3 are the king's, but they are not his to spend on himself. Every appetite that a ruler indulges has a victim, and in verse 5 the victims are named: the oppressed who lose their case because the judge forgot the law.

Second, a person's worst failures are often the quiet ones. The mother does not warn against tyranny or war. She warns against what a bored or pampered man might drift into. By starting with the bedroom and the cup, the oracle shows that justice is lost in small private habits before it is lost in the court.

Third, speech is a form of power that belongs to those who have it. The king's duty is not only to avoid harm but to use his mouth. The poor in Israel could not litigate for themselves, and to the first hearers the instruction was very concrete: if you sit at the gate or on the throne, speak for the person who cannot, and judge by what is right, not by who is rich.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage prescribes. The mother gives commands to her son: do not spend, do not drink, open your mouth, judge righteously, defend. These are not observations about what kings usually do. They are the standard against which kings are to be measured, and the book of Proverbs expects readers to take them seriously.

The one place where care is needed is the permission in verses 6 and 7. The mother says to give strong drink to the one perishing and wine to the bitter in soul. This is not a command for believers to numb sorrow with alcohol, and it is not a general permission for drunkenness. It is a contrast within a speech about kings: for a ruler, whose judgment other people depend on, drink is forbidden; for a suffering person, it can be an act of mercy, a kind of anaesthetic. Elsewhere the Bible never makes drunkenness a remedy for grief. Believers apply the passage by reading verses 6 and 7 as a hard-edged picture of compassion at a deathbed, not as a prescription, and by letting verses 8 and 9, the call to action, carry the weight of the passage.

The warning is written to a king but it applies by extension. Anyone who holds a judgment seat, a vote, a workplace or a pulpit can ask whether appetite is clouding a duty owed to the weak.

debates.question: What is the point of verses 6 and 7, giving strong drink to the perishing?

views.label: Mercy toward the dying and the grieving
views.case: The verses sit against the king's prohibition in verses 4 and 5 as a deliberate contrast. A man facing death or deep bitterness of soul, the phrase Job uses in Job 3:20, may be given drink to dull the pain, while the ruler, whose clear judgment others depend on, may not. Jesus Himself was offered wine mixed with myrrh before the cross, Mark 15:23, which reads as a similar act of mercy, though He refused it. On this view the mother is describing compassion, not recommending escape.

views.label: Ironic or bitter counsel
views.case: Some read the lines as irony. If drink is all the poor are given instead of justice, then the king's failure turns the dispossessed into people who forget their misery in a cup. The next verse then answers with the better gift, a mouth open for them. This reading takes the verses as a rebuke of how rulers treat the poor and not as advice.

views.label: A general permission for drink
views.case: A few read the lines as a general approval of alcohol for those who are not rulers. That fits other texts that speak of wine gladdening the heart, but it stretches a short aside into a principle the oracle does not state and which would cut against Proverbs 20:1.

debates.bearing: The oracle puts its weight on verses 8 and 9, not on the aside. All three readings agree that the king may not drink away his duty, and none makes alcohol a solution to suffering. The safest application is mercy for the suffering and sobriety for those who hold other people's lives in their hands.

debates.question: Who is Lemuel, and does his identity matter?

views.label: Solomon under another name
views.case: Jewish and Christian tradition has often identified Lemuel with Solomon, with Bathsheba as the mother who taught him, since the book is so closely tied to Solomon. The name may then be a pet name, the Hebrew sounding like 'belonging to God'. The advantage is that it places the oracle in Israel's own court.

views.label: A foreign king, perhaps of Massa
views.case: The text never calls Lemuel king of Israel, and Proverbs 30:1 gives Agur a similarly unnamed background. If 'Massa' in verse 1 is a place and not the word 'burden', Lemuel was a king in northern Arabia, and the book includes wisdom from beyond Israel's borders.

views.label: An otherwise unknown Israelite or royal figure
views.case: Others say the text simply tells us all we can know, that he is a king whose mother is the source, and that the name is not given any clue. The oracle works the same way whoever he was.

debates.bearing: The meaning of the oracle does not depend on solving the question. It teaches about a mother, a king and the poor, and that holds in all three cases. The honest answer is that Scripture does not tell us who Lemuel was.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 calls the speech a massa, the 'burden' or 'oracle'. The word is built on a verb meaning to lift or carry, and it is the same word that heads many prophetic messages in Isaiah and Nahum, so it carries a sense of weighty utterance. Whether it should here be read as a place name, Massa, is a real question, as the Ishmaelite name in Genesis 25:14 shows, but the BSB and most English versions take it as a common noun. In either case the oracle is introduced as something borne, not casually offered.

Verse 2 uses an unusual word for 'son' three times. The ordinary Hebrew word is ben, but this verse has bar, which is the Aramaic word for son, as in Psalm 2:12. That is a hint of the foreign or archaic flavour of the oracle. The three phrases, 'my son', 'son of my womb', 'son of my vows', rise from the plain to the intimate to the sacred. The third points to a vow, the kind of promise a mother makes to God for a child, as Hannah did in 1 Samuel 1:11, though the text does not say what Lemuel's mother vowed. The BSB footnote notes that the opening could also be read 'What are you doing?', which would make the mother's speech a rebuke from the start.

In verse 3, the king's 'strength' comes from the same root as chayil, the word that will describe the capable woman in verse 10. Her strength is spent well; the king's is in danger of being spent on 'those who ruin kings', a phrase whose verb means to wipe out.

Verse 5 warns the king against forgetting 'what is decreed'. The Hebrew is from the root choq, a word for something inscribed, a statute or a limit. It is the vocabulary of law, not mere custom, and the thing forgotten is the standing written word that protects the weak. The people deprived are the 'oppressed', literally sons of affliction, which names them by their condition.

In verse 6 the person 'perishing' and the one 'bitter in soul' are placed side by side. The second phrase is the same idiom used by Job in Job 3:20 and it names someone whose inner life is soured by grief.

Verses 8 and 9 begin with the same command, 'open your mouth'. The first object is 'those with no voice', from the Hebrew for mute, and the second is the cause of the 'dispossessed', a phrase whose exact sense is debated but which clearly names people who have lost what they once had. Verse 9 then adds two judicial verbs, 'judge righteously' and 'defend the cause', and the word tzedek, righteousness, is the very standard that Psalm 72:1-2 asks God to give the king.

typology.type: The queen mother as teacher, Proverbs 31:1
typology.fulfillment: A mother's instruction shapes a future king, and the picture reaches forward to Mary, who taught and watched over the child who would be King. Luke records her pondering and treasuring what she saw, Luke 2:19, 51. The escalation lies in the Son: where Lemuel receives instruction on how to rule, Jesus learns obedience and increases in wisdom, Luke 2:52, and then rules in perfect justice. The type falls short because Lemuel needed warning against failure, while the true Son of Mary never fails.

typology.type: The king who opens his mouth for the voiceless, Proverbs 31:8-9
typology.fulfillment: The king is to be the advocate of those who cannot plead for themselves. Isaiah promises a King who will judge the poor 'with righteousness' and decide 'with equity' for the lowly of the earth, Isaiah 11:4. Jesus fulfils it in His own preaching to the poor, Luke 4:18, and His final advocacy is as the one who intercedes for His people, Hebrews 7:25, and who is their advocate with the Father, 1 John 2:1. The type is outstripped because Lemuel can only speak for the poor in court, while Christ speaks for sinners before God.

typology.type: The sober king who keeps his judgment clear, Proverbs 31:4-5
typology.fulfillment: The king may not drink lest he forget the decree and wrong the oppressed. At the cross Jesus refused the wine mixed with myrrh, Mark 15:23, and at the Last Supper He vowed not to drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes, Mark 14:25. He kept His mind clear to carry out the Father's will to the end. The correspondence is real, though the passage does not mention the cross, and the link is an inference from the pattern of the king who will not numb himself.

study.christ:
The oracle leads to Christ first by describing the kind of king the whole Bible is waiting for. Lemuel's mother does not ask for a successful king or a famous king. She asks for one who guards his strength, keeps a clear mind and gives his voice to people who have none. When Psalm 72 prays for the king to 'save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor', Psalm 72:4, it asks for the same thing, and Isaiah 11:3-5 promises a ruler who does not judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear but with righteousness for the poor, with righteousness as the belt around his hips. The Gospels present Jesus as exactly that king. He reads Isaiah in the synagogue and says that the good news to the poor is fulfilled in their hearing, Luke 4:18-21.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the failed kings. Solomon, the wisest of Israel's rulers, spent his vigor on many wives who turned his heart, 1 Kings 11:1-4, and the poor of his later reign paid for it. Jesus, by contrast, is offered every kingdom of the world and refuses to be turned aside, Matthew 4:8-10. He does not take a bride from the world but gives Himself up for the church, Ephesians 5:25. Where the oracle warns against the cup that makes a ruler forget, He took the cup the Father gave Him, John 18:11, and remembered every person He came to save.

It leads to Christ by His speech. The voiceless in the Gospels are many: the woman caught in adultery whose accusers stand ready, the man born blind who is thrown out, the children whom the disciples send away. In each case Jesus opens His mouth for them. In the end He speaks for all the powerless before God, for He 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25. The vulnerable who have no voice before the Judge have an advocate who speaks first.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The oracle is a plain piece of moral instruction to a human king, and it is not a hidden prophecy. The link to Christ rests on the pattern it sets for righteous rule and on the New Testament's own portrait of Jesus as that ruler, not on any allegory of the wine or the mother. What the passage supplies is a standard of kingship, and Christ is the king who meets it completely.
study.god:
The passage shows God by what He demands of those who stand in His place. The ruler is to treat the poor and needy as God treats them, and the closeness of the instruction to the character of God is the point. Proverbs 22:22-23 says why: 'the LORD will take up their case.' The LORD is the real defender of the weak, and a king who defends them is acting as His deputy. The one who crushes the poor stands against God Himself.

It shows God as a God of justice who cares about the details of a courtroom. The decree that the king must not forget is not a private rule of the court but a standard that matters to God. Psalm 82:3-4 rebukes unjust judges in God's own assembly and tells them to defend the weak and the fatherless and rescue the needy from the hand of the wicked. A holy God is never indifferent to who gets a fair hearing.

It shows God as one who cares about the whole person of the ruler. The passage connects bedroom, table and throne. God does not divide a man into a private self and a public self. He sees that appetite unchecked in private damages the lives of strangers in public. The same God who commands justice in the city asks for self-control in the heart.

There is also tenderness. The permission in verses 6 and 7 is a note of pity for the dying and the bitter in soul. Scripture elsewhere describes God as close to those who suffer. Job's phrase 'bitter of soul', Job 3:20, is spoken to a God who does not turn away from lament. And the setting of the whole speech, a mother's care, echoes the way God Himself compares His comfort to a mother's, Isaiah 66:13.

For worship, the passage turns every reader's attention to the God who hears people who cannot speak. We pray to a King who does not need to be told about the voiceless, because He sees them already, and the response He asks of His people is not only gratitude but imitation. To worship such a God and ignore the powerless is to contradict what we sing.

crossReferences.note: Agur's words open with the same title, the 'burden' or oracle, so the last two chapters of the book are twin appendices. Agur confesses his weariness and ignorance, then Lemuel's mother gives a command. Together they show that wisdom is both humble before God and active toward the poor.

The law of the king forbids him to take many wives lest his heart go astray, and it warns against hoarding silver and gold. Lemuel's mother puts the same fence around her son in the language of a household. The Torah and the queen mother say the same thing, and Solomon's life shows what happens when it is ignored.

This is the story of what happened when a wise king ignored this warning. Solomon clung to many foreign women, and they turned his heart after other gods. It is the closest narrative illustration of verse 3, and it explains why Proverbs ends with a king being told the lesson in advance.

The prophet pronounces woe on those who are heroes in drinking wine while they acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice. It is the courtroom side of verses 4 and 5, showing that the fear of the mother is the actual condition of Isaiah's Judah.

This is the voice of verse 8 in other words: rescue those led away to death, and do not plead ignorance, for the God who weighs hearts knows. It adds a sobering reason to the king's duty, because the one who sees and does nothing will answer to the LORD.

The royal prayer for Solomon asks God to give the king His justice so that he judges the afflicted with righteousness and crushes the oppressor. The prayer and the oracle describe the same ideal king from two sides, one as the prayer of the nation and the other as the lesson of a mother.

Job, defending his righteousness, says he was eyes to the blind, feet to the lame and a father to the needy, and that he took up the case of the stranger. It is a portrait of a man who actually opened his mouth for the powerless, and it shows that the duty is not for kings alone.

The coming shoot from Jesse will not judge by sight or hearsay but with righteousness for the poor and equity for the lowly. The prophecy lifts the oracle's ideal into a promise about a particular King, and it gives the reader a reason to look beyond Lemuel.

Jesus reads that He is anointed to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim liberty to the captives and to release the oppressed. The Servant-King takes the cause of the voiceless as His mission and does what the oracle asks of every ruler.

Offered wine mixed with myrrh at the cross, Jesus did not take it. It recalls the contrast of verses 4 to 7, a ruler who stays clear-minded for the sake of those he serves, though the Gospel does not tie the two texts together and the link is a reading of the pattern.

Jesus always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God. The great advocate of the voiceless now stands before the Father on behalf of people who cannot plead their own case, which is the heavenly side of the king's earthly duty in verses 8 and 9.

study.oneStory:
The oracle answers a question left open since the days of Genesis: who will rule the world for the good of the weak? Humanity was made to exercise dominion, Genesis 1:26-28, and the first human rulers used their strength to oppress. Cain's descendant Lamech boasted of his violence, Genesis 4:23-24. From the beginning, the powerful tend to spend their strength on themselves, and the cry of the poor goes up. The oracle is a mother's attempt to turn one king away from that path.

After the fall, God's answer is a line of kings who are meant to reverse it. The law of the king, Deuteronomy 17:14-20, fences off the ruler's appetites, and the royal psalms pray for a king who will save the needy. Israel's history shows how often the kings failed. Solomon's slide into many wives, 1 Kings 11:1-4, is the best-known example, and the prophets condemn rulers who feasted while the poor were crushed, Isaiah 5:22-23. The oracle is therefore not abstract advice. It is a warning that history confirmed, and it sits at the end of Proverbs as a final test of whether wisdom has become practice.

The story does not rest on human kings. It looks toward the King promised in Isaiah 11, who judges the poor with righteousness. Jesus comes as that King. He announces good news to the poor, refuses the cup that would dull His purpose, and gives Himself instead of taking from others, Philippians 2:6-8. His kingdom is marked by the reversal that the oracle commands: the voiceless are heard, the dispossessed receive an inheritance and the powerful are made servants.

The church lives between that victory and its completion. Believers are called a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, and share in the work of speaking for the weak. The pattern of the oracle is extended from kings to every person with any power at all, whether in a home, a workplace or a congregation.

The story ends with a world where the King's justice is complete. In the new creation the nations walk by His light and there is no more crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. No one will need an advocate because the Judge Himself will wipe every tear. Until then, the oracle's call to open our mouths is part of how God's kingdom is already breaking in.

quiz.q: Who instructed King Lemuel according to verse 1?

options.text: His mother.
options.note: This oracle is explicitly credited to a queen mother's teaching.

options.text: His father, the previous king.
options.note: The text names his mother, not his father, as the source of this instruction.

options.text: A court prophet.
options.note: No prophet is named as the source; the instruction is maternal.

options.text: An unnamed group of royal advisors.
options.note: The text specifically credits one person, his mother, not a group of advisors.

quiz.q: What warning does verse 4-5 give a king about wine?

options.text: It is not for kings to drink wine, lest they forget what is decreed and deprive the oppressed of justice.
options.note: A king's clarity of mind is directly tied to protecting justice for the vulnerable.

options.text: Kings should drink freely to relax from the burdens of rule.
options.note: This is the opposite of the warning given.

options.text: Wine is forbidden for everyone, not just kings.
options.note: The warning here specifically addresses kings and rulers, not a universal prohibition.

options.text: Wine is acceptable for kings only during festivals.
options.note: The text gives no such festival exception; its concern is the king's ongoing responsibility for justice.

quiz.q: What does verse 8 charge the king to do?

options.text: Open his mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed.
options.note: The king's authority is to be used specifically on behalf of the voiceless.

options.text: Remain silent on matters of justice to avoid controversy.
options.note: This is the opposite of the charge given.

options.text: Speak primarily in defense of his own royal interests.
options.note: The charge is explicitly to defend others, especially the dispossessed, not himself.

options.text: Delegate all matters of justice to lower officials.
options.note: The charge is a direct, personal responsibility given to the king himself, not a call to delegate it away.

quiz.q: What does verse 9 add to the charge of opening the mouth?

options.text: Judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy.
options.note: Righteous judgment and active defense of the vulnerable are paired together.

options.text: Judge according to the wealth of those involved.
options.note: This is the opposite of righteous judgment as described.

options.text: Avoid making any judgments at all.
options.note: The verse specifically calls for judging, not avoiding judgment.

options.text: Judge quickly without full consideration of the facts.
options.note: The verse calls for righteous judgment, which implies careful fairness, not mere speed.

quiz.q: What does verse 3 warn against regarding women?

options.text: Spending your strength on women who ruin kings.
options.note: The warning targets destructive relationships that corrupt a king's strength and rule, not women generally.

options.text: Ever marrying at all.
options.note: This is not the point of the warning; marriage itself is not condemned here.

options.text: Listening to any counsel from women.
options.note: This oracle is itself maternal counsel that the king is meant to heed, contradicting this option.

options.text: Having daughters as heirs.
options.note: This is not the subject of the verse; the warning concerns self-destructive indulgence, not succession.

questions: This oracle is a mother's urgent instruction to her royal son. What wisdom from a parent or mentor have you received that still shapes you today?
Verses 4-5 warn that a king's indulgence directly harms the oppressed who depend on his justice. Where might your own private habits be quietly affecting your ability to serve others well?
Verse 8 charges the king to open his mouth for those with no voice. Who around you currently has no voice, and what would it look like for you to speak up on their behalf?
Verse 9 calls for judging righteously and defending the poor and needy. Where in your own sphere of influence, family, work, community, are you being called to greater fairness?
This whole oracle points forward to Christ, the King who emptied Himself for others rather than indulging Himself. Where do you need to trade self-indulgence for self-giving this week?

translationNotes.note: 'The burden' translates massa, which can mean either a prophetic oracle or, following an alternate vocalization favored by some scholars, could relate to a place name, Massa, mentioned in Genesis 25:14; most translations, including the BSB, favor the sense of a solemn oracle or utterance here.

'Son of my vows' likely refers to a vow the mother made to God concerning this child, perhaps similar to Hannah's vow concerning Samuel, 1 Samuel 1:11, underscoring the weight and seriousness of her instruction.

This exception for giving strong drink to the perishing stands in deliberate contrast to the king's own required sobriety in verses 4-5, sharpening rather than softening the warning against royal self-indulgence.
